rationale: flops-3 is a tiny, floating-point-arithmetic-dominated kernel from SingleSource whose entire execution is a hot numeric loop, so runtime overhead is the binding constraint while code size matters little and static features (no source lines, unknown function count) offer little to reason about. SUB is the workhorse here: it transforms the FP/integer arithmetic that constitutes the whole program, is semantically safe, and adds negligible cost, so it gets the highest priority with low cost/risk weights. BCF provides strong control-flow concealment but its opaque predicates would run on every loop iteration of a compute-bound kernel, so despite high security gain it carries deliberately high RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights to suppress aggressive application; FLA is similarly throttled because flattening a single tight loop adds dispatcher overhead with little to hide and carries nontrivial correctness risk on FP control flow. SPLIT is cheap and safe and is kept at moderate diversity weight to add basic-block-level variety at essentially zero cost. IBR gets a balanced profile: it meaningfully diversifies the branch-heavy loop structure at moderate cost, making it the best security-per-overhead control-flow pass for this kernel. ICALL is de-emphasized since a numeric kernel has few indirect-call opportunities and the indirection costs register pressure and dispersion in a hot loop, with moderate risk on FP-heavy code; IGV is kept mild because flops-3 contains few integer constants worth obscuring, though it remains safe and inexpensive enough to leave enabled.
